Anthropic's IPO roadshow video. Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works.

The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs.
I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below:

We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...]
As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention. Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...]
The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units.
Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself, allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster.
We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues, where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments.

articles.title: Glue work is still harmful in the age of AI
articles.titleZh: Glue work is still harmful in the age of AI
articles.summary: Glue work is still harmful in the age of AI

blocks.text: I am not a believer in glue work1. Processes that can only be sustained by the unrewarded sacrifice of engineers ought to die.

Now that LLMs are writing most of our code, does that free human engineers up to do more glue work? No, it doesn’t. I think glue work is actually less important to companies than it was in the 2010s. Let’s go through four reasons why.

First, AI decreases the amount of coordination needed to ship. The magnifying effect of AI agents means that any single engineer can now take on projects that would previously have needed a small team. A lot of glue work was helping with coordination: booking kickoff and status meetings, passing around internal updates, and so on. A single engineer doesn’t need to do any of that.

Second, engineers in the 2020s require less “careful handling”. In my experience, the most important subcategory of coordination-based glue work was managing difficult people. Many companies have secret gatekeepers: engineers with outsized influence and large egos who will shoot down your project if they feel insufficiently consulted. I’ve written before about how some teams are structurally set up to be gatekeepers, and how some engineers could get by in the 2010s by basically saying no to everything. The end of ZIRP changed all that. Many of the prickliest gatekeepers have been forced out of the industry or coerced into changing their attitude, which reduces the amount of necessary glue work required to ship.

Third, people are hiring fewer juniors. This is probably a bad thing for the industry, but it does also eliminate a big category of glue work. Experienced hires need less hand-holding, so companies don’t need people to quietly volunteer to onboard new hires.

Fourth, write-only reports can be automated with LLMs. A lot of glue work was what I call “proof of work”: writing a report to demonstrate that you’re aware of what your team is doing, or filling in a template to satisfy some legal requirement. This was often work that nobody wanted to do, so it relied on someone volunteering to “be glue”. Now reports like these can be quickly turned out with LLMs. It doesn’t really matter that nobody wants to read LLM text, because the point of these reports was never to be read anyway.

Can LLMs just automate all glue work? Absolutely not. Many engineers are trying to do this out of a kind of manic optimism, but it’s a really bad idea. Write-only reports are one thing, but communicating to other engineers cannot be delegated to an LLM. When you need to check in on the status of a project, or respond to someone else’s ping, or anything like that, you should compose and write the message yourself. Nothing will torch your relationship with other engineers as quickly as making them talk to your Claude Opus instance.

So where does that leave us? More or less where we were in 2024, I think. Avoid at all costs becoming “the glue work person”, let bad processes fail so they can be changed, but be willing to do small amounts of tactical glue work where it can meaningfully contribute to the success of your projects. Most of your time and effort should still be spent on the code: on driving AI agents and aligning them with your company’s values.

Glue work is all the squishy “non-technical” work that goes into building software: making sure teams are talking to each other, writing reports, updating docs, onboarding engineers, and so on. Specifically it’s the parts of that work that are not included in the formal process, and that only really get done if someone volunteers to do it. For more on why I don’t like it, see my 2024 post Glue work considered harmful.

articles.title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
articles.titleZh: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
articles.summary: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?

blocks.text: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).
The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with ransomware groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].
The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.
Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: Gang Exposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

articles.title: Apple Shutters Their Longstanding ‘Apple Support Community’
articles.titleZh: Apple Shutters Their Longstanding ‘Apple Support Community’
articles.summary: Apple Shutters Their Longstanding ‘Apple Support Community’

blocks.text: In a long-overdue move, Apple has brought down the hammer on its “Apple Support Community” forum. As Joe Rossignol at MacRumors reports:

Apple’s full notice added to the site: “The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site. We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.”
  It is the end of an era. Apple offered an online discussion forum for user-to-user technical support since 1998, when it launched the Apple Tech Exchange. The forums were renamed to Apple Discussions in 2000, and then to the Apple Support Communities in 2011, before taking on their current Apple Support Community name in 2022.
  Apple informed MacRumors that it decided to sunset the Apple Support Community after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs.

These message boards were an embarrassment for Apple. Not only were they very much out of step with what the web has come to be over the last couple of decades, but their presence under an apple.com domain meant that they ranked highly in search and were perceived by the general public as being official in some way.

But they weren’t, nor were they helpful. They were full of people asking questions and not getting useful answers, with many responses given by users who were more motivated to gain karma in the forum’s user-ranking system than to help. I can’t tell you how many times I visited these forums while trying to track down the answer to a peculiar quirk or bug, only to find the (legitimate!) question being shut down by an officious high-ranking know-it-all who didn’t actually understand what was being asked and couldn’t provide a useful answer.
Good riddance.

blocks.text: A week with the iPhone Duo at home, camping and in Iceland. A capable camera with new tricks, and a creative powerhouse for planning, editing and sharing.
Hi from Iceland!
In the last week, I’ve had a lot of fun getting to know the iPhone Duo at home, camping with family and yesterday I arrived in Iceland to guide some friends on a private tour.

Honestly, the idea of a folding iPhone didn’t immediately appeal to me. I usually like smaller devices, but when I first started playing with the Duo in September, I realized it’s really something special and I couldn’t wait to get my hands on a review unit from Apple. The iPhone 18 Pro remains the most powerful camera in the lineup, and though the Duo also has an excellent camera, where it really shines is everything around the photograph: planning, editing and sharing.
I always approach these projects with one question, and though the camera isn’t the whole story here, it’s still my question:
HOW DOES THIS NEW TECH MAKE MY PHOTOS AND VIDEOS BETTER?

As I’ve looked to answer this question, I haven’t been able to go all-in on a dedicated shoot like I usually do for my camera reviews, but I learned a lot just having the Duo with me as I work, shoot and travel.
Let’s jump in.
After my iPhone 18 Pro Camera Review, many of you asked for more insight so I’m releasing my iPhone 18 Pro Camera Field Guide on November 1st, sign up here to be the first to know when it drops.
Aurora over southern Iceland. Night mode, no tripod, Duo in seated positioniPhone Duo26mm1xƒ/1.65sISO 5000
No tripod needed

You never know when the aurora might show itself and though I almost always have my Ultrapod + Glif tripod with me, sometimes it’s back in the room when needed! Last night in the parking lot of our hotel in southern Iceland, the aurora started dancing in the sky. I partially opened the iPhone Duo, set it on top of the car and used Night mode and was able to capture the aurora overhead without ever fiddling with a tripod. What a moment in iPhone photography history!

The iPhone camera team is always looking for ways to eliminate the need for additional hardware (integrating lenses, building Action mode so no gimbal is needed, etc) and this is a BIG one. The iPhone Duo can now shoot long exposures in Night mode without a tripod!
Smart Take
I’ve found Smart Take works surprisingly well. Apple says “it follows the scene in real time and automatically snaps the photo when everyone is posed and ready,” and it does.

We went camping this weekend and while Olivia and I were playing on a merry-go-round at the campground I decided to try it out. I partially opened the Duo, set it on the ground in laptop-style mode (no tripod needed), set it to Smart Take and sat down with Olivia. The Duo waited til we were both looking at the camera (which of course took a second for Olivia) and then snapped automatically.
Olivia and me on the merry-go-round, captured by Smart TakeiPhone Duo26mm1x12MPƒ/1.61/7000ISO 200
Anyone with kids knows how tough it can be to get a young kid to look at the camera, so I think this feature is going to be super popular.
To turn on Smart Take, open the Camera and tap the Grid icon in the lower right to reveal camera settings, choose Smart Take.
Traveling with Duo
Duo has been handy while traveling.
Shooting in the folded position. Photo of the Duo made with iPhone 18 ProiPhone 18 Pro24mm1x18MPƒ/1.51/80ISO 250
Descending on the approach to IcelandiPhone Duo52mm2xƒ/1.61/60ISO 100
My favorite travel app Flighty has been updated for Duo and looks beautiful on the big display.
Flighty on the Duo’s inner displayiPhone Duo

The seated configuration is super handy for watching movies in transit. Icelandair has always screened The Secret Life of Walter Mitty on their flights, but since I flew Delta this time, I watched on my iPhone Duo to continue the tradition.
The Secret Life of Walter Mitty on the Duo, somewhere over the Atlantic. Photo of the Duo made with iPhone 18 ProiPhone 18 Pro24mm1x18MPƒ/1.51/45ISO 500
The nano-texture display
As you may know, I've always been a fan of matte, nano-texture displays… even at the cost of a little vibrance, I prefer no reflections.
The inner display on the Duo looks lovely and feels great to the touch. It works well in bright sun, and I imagine it will feel paper-like with Apple Pencil.
The crease is visible from an angle if you look for it, but I didn’t notice it in daily use.
Schoolhouse on the Kansas prairieiPhone Duo26mm1xƒ/1.61/3200ISO 32
Same IP68 water resistance as 18 Pro

I was surprised to learn that the iPhone Duo has the same IP68 water resistance rating as the iPhone 18 Pro. The hinge is impressive enough, but keeping it water resistant seems like an incredible feat of engineering. I took the Duo into the drenched canyon at Gljúfrabúi and made this photo of Nathan and Paige with the Duo soaked in mist.
Gljúfrabúi, with the Duo absolutely drenched in mistiPhone Duo26mm1x18MPƒ/1.61/121ISO 80
Shooting with Duo
The Duo’s hardware opens up a handful of new shooting positions.

I’ve found folded to be best: one hand, discreet, fastest from pocket to shot. You can also shoot unfolded, which looks gorgeous on the big display, but I find the camera harder to operate that way and it really draws attention to you.

The all-new trick is partially folded, which feels a bit like shooting top down with an old Rolleiflex. You can shoot outward while looking down or up at the device, which is great for staying discreet and for really low and high angles like the image below. I found myself drawn to this shooting style as it feels really different than most iPhone photography.
Shot low to the road from partially-folded mode, southern IcelandiPhone Duo14mm0.5xƒ/2.21/500ISO 50
Sharing with Duo

One of the things I love about iPad is how it thrives at sharing photos, and the Duo has the same quality. It’s easy to pass to a friend, images look stunning on the display, and the platform just naturally lends itself to sharing.
Nathan and Paige on the coast, IcelandiPhone Duo14mm0.5x24MPƒ/2.21/750ISO 32
Kid Cue and Duo Preview

The native Camera app has two new features that use the outer display while shooting. Open the Duo, open the Camera app on the inner display and tap the new icon in the top right. Kid Cue plays Snoopy to pull a kid’s attention to the camera. Duo Preview shows a live preview on the outer display to whoever is in front of your camera.
Kid Cue playing Snoopy on the outer display. Photo of the Duo made with iPhone 17 Pro MaxiPhone 17 Pro Max24mm1xƒ/2.21/30ISO 125
Duo Preview means you can now shoot selfies with the 48MP camera and a live preview, something no other iPhone can do.
A few thoughts for serious creative pros
Pro retouchers will love using Apple Pencil on the Duo for masking and selections, especially on the paper-like nano-texture screen.

Both displays use the new Color Matching Function (CMF) technology released with 18 Pro, which means better color accuracy and consistency for anyone using multiple devices in their creative workflow.

ProRAW is not supported in the native Camera app on iPhone Duo, and it’s unclear to me why. I rarely use ProRAW because I prefer the power and speed of Photographic Styles, but I do use it in low light to control noise reduction. To shoot aurora like the image above, I’d normally be in ProRAW.
For now you need a third-party app to shoot RAW on the Duo. Apple recommends Afterlight, Moment Pro Camera II, Halide Pro Camera III and Not Boring Camera, which all support it.

I migrated all my settings and apps from my 18 Pro and every camera setting came over except one: Preserve Settings > Resolution. I set the Duo to 48MP and it kept switching back to 24MP until I revisited Settings > Preserve Settings and realized that setting hadn’t transferred from my iPhone 18 Pro because on the Duo it has a slightly different title.

The Duo hasn’t been my main daily device, but I’ve pushed it hard shooting and editing photos, planning my trip, outlining ideas and watching movies, and the battery has been consistently better than I expected.
I haven’t been able to test this yet but I’m looking forward to having the Duo in my pocket to use it as a tether monitor connected to my Hasselblad/Sony etc.
Creative apps on iPhone Duo

Esther has played piano her whole life and we’ve been wanting to get Olivia started… that serendipitously happened on a Saturday morning when I downloaded the new PianoFold app for iPhone Duo and set it in front of Olivia, who is almost 4.
She picked it up immediately and I eventually had to take it away, she was having so much fun.
Not Boring Camera emulates an analog camera and offers a bunch of filmic looks.
Procreate Pocket is fully optimized for iPhone Duo and, with Apple Pencil support, will be a popular on-the-go sketchbook for hand-drawn artists.
Tide Guide is a beautiful, simple app for planning around the tide.

These are just a few of the earliest apps designed for Duo, but I absolutely can't wait to see the creative ideas developers come up with to really leverage this completely new hardware configuration.
A few wishes
I’d like the native Camera app to be able to use the outer display as a flash, the way Photo Booth flashes the whole screen. It could be a big, soft light source, especially nice for portraits.
ProRAW in the native Camera app! It’d be super useful for aurora and other RAW use cases.
Smart Take across the rest of the iPhone lineup. It’s a compelling feature for capturing the perfect moment and it’d be super popular.
The south coast of IcelandiPhone Duo14mm0.5x18MPƒ/2.21/750ISO 32
The Bottom Line

The iPhone Duo offers a great camera, more than enough for most users and for me in most situations. Creative pros will miss the longer lens, but gain a big, beautiful display, the freedom to shoot without a tripod, and entirely new ways to capture, edit and share images.

The Duo represents perhaps the most exciting innovation in iPhone hardware since, dare I say, the original iPhone. It’s a joy to shoot with and an even more powerful companion throughout my creative workflow, from planning shoots with Sunlitt to editing in Lightroom and outlining in MindNode. It’s earned a place in my core kit, and I’m genuinely excited to see where this new chapter of the iPhone takes us.

articles.title: HowTo: Fix Eufy HomeBase 2 Storage Full Issues
articles.titleZh: HowTo: Fix Eufy HomeBase 2 Storage Full Issues
articles.summary: HowTo: Fix Eufy HomeBase 2 Storage Full Issues

blocks.text: Quick Fix: Insert a USB memory stick, format it in the app, restart the Eufy HomeBase 2, format the internal memory, restart the hub.
Background

I've had the eufyCam system for over 6 years - which is pretty long-life for IoT devices.  The cameras have worked pretty much flawlessly. Four years ago I added their Video Doorbell which has been similarly well behaved.

But last night I went to check some security footage, only to be told that the 16GB storage was full. Ordinarily that shouldn't be a problem. Full storage just means that older videos get wiped and new ones replace them. In my case, all the old videos were gone.
I could see the cameras and control them, I just couldn't access any old recordings.
There was nothing on there I especially needed (although I'm curious as to when a courier dropped off a "lost" parcel) so I was happy to experiment with fixing the system.

The Eufy forums are full of people having these issues. Anker, the brand that own Eufy are usually fairly customer focused - but I guess they're more interested in getting people to upgrade to a newer hub than fixing the problems with their old kit.
What Didn't Work
Restarting - no change.
Repairing the storage - didn't fix anything.
Clearing the storage - dire warnings but didn't help.
Formatting - a last resort, but failed.
What Fixed It
I found an old 4GB USB-A memory stick and shoved it in the back of the Eufy. The app detected it fairly quickly and said the stick needed to be formatted - so I let it.

Once the stick was formatted, I restarted the hub. Running fix or clean didn't change the situation, so I tried formatting the main memory again. This time it seemed to work. It crawled to 100% and then hung.
I restarted the app and it told me that the storage was unformatted and needed to be formatted again, so I let it.
I restarted the hub and everything sprang to life, no more warnings about full storage.
Next Steps
I'll keep an eye on the storage to make sure it doesn't fill up again.

I'm reluctant to buy a new HomeBase. I like to self-host things, but the promise of commercial kit like this is that it takes the hassle out of ownership. I don't really want to be futzing around formatting memory and deciphering error messages.
If this fails again, I'll have to seriously consider moving my cameras onto something that I can control. At least that way, if it screws up, I'll only have myself to blame.

Archives
Categories
Blogroll

20 years ago to this day, I started my new technical blog.  I'd had a personal one
for some time, but most of the stuff that happened there had already migrated to
social media.  I wanted somewhere to post the things that would only
be of interest to my techier friends, and maybe of some use to anyone else that
came across it.

Things have changed a bit, but they've stayed the same in some ways.  Earlier
this year I finished my 48-part (!) LLM from scratch
series, but it had predecessors -- the third post I made here was
part one of a 13-part series
where I worked through setting up automated backups for my homelab NAS, and then later on
I spent a few months building a reverse proxy in C, not to mention the eight-month, ten-post
series on fine-tuning LLMs.

It does seem like there's some value to putting all of this online.  I rarely check
my logs and referrers, but people do still seem to be arriving here having searched
for stuff that I've written about, and every now and then there's a kind "thanks for this!" comment
left on an old post where I explained something I'd just learned.

I wrote a bit more about the blog's history last
year, and came to the conclusion that the best posts -- both for me to write, and as
far as I could tell for other people to read -- were the ones where I wrote up
a project that I'd been working on.  I blogged about that in more detail,
and it seemed to strike a chord on Hacker News; I think it still holds.

Recently, Sean Goedecke suggested
that the best blog posts are those where you write about things that you're in the process of learning, and
I agree.  You learn more than you would if you didn't write it up, and because things
are fresh in your mind, you may well write more clearly about it than an actual
expert in the subject might have done.

Anyway, I'm going to carry on blogging.  I'm working on my biggest LLM-related project
so far (dozens of training runs, so my study aircon is getting quite the workout even
with the weather turning colder), and look forward to posting about it later on this month.
I hope it's at least as fun to read as it is to write!

articles.title: Why Am I So Tired If AI Is Doing All the Work?
articles.titleZh: Why Am I So Tired If AI Is Doing All the Work?
articles.summary: Why Am I So Tired If AI Is Doing All the Work?

blocks.text: There’s this concept in Computer Science called thrashing. The tl;dr is that thrashing can happen when programs running on a computer are actively using more memory than can fit in RAM. The OS will keep moving data between memory and disk, making room for something by removing something else (that it will need again shortly). And, at some point, so much time goes into moving things around that the programs barely make any real progress.

Boy, oh boy, isn’t that every single one of us right now using AI? One agent is working, and you, almost by reflex, will start something else. Kind of like doomscrolling: you don’t even realize you’re doing it.

And by the way, of course we’re doing it! These apps (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, etc.) make it so easy to keep several things going at once. It feels silly to be sitting there watching the agent build your thing while you’re just passively watching.
But I think this exact behavior is what’s making a lot of us feel exhausted at the end of the day. Mostly because of that last part: multitasking.

Because when the agent comes back, you need to understand what it did before you can do anything useful with it. blocks.text: This week’s version control and forge news, gathered from release feeds for source control clients and forges, the Lobsters vcs tag, Hacker News, and my boosts on Mastodon. Package management news is in the Saturday This Week in Package Management roundup.
Scaling

Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture (Karthik Raman and Brian Celenza, GitHub) describes Rubicon, the design announced at GitHub Universe. Packs go to Azure Blob Storage. References and the list of packs are stored in Ref-CAS, a replicated log service where each reference update is a compare-and-swap committed by a quorum, so a push waits only on other pushes to the same reference. In internal tests one repository accepted 7,200 pushes per second from 5,000 concurrent agents.

Requests still arrive at Spokes, which routes each one to a small group of virtual replicas, disposable compute nodes whose local disk is a cache. A replica handling a write indexes the pack, uploads it to Blob Storage, then commits one Ref-CAS transaction. For reads it sends the version in its cache, and the reply includes references only if they have changed since that version.

Two earlier prototypes stored reference state in blobs. The first, a write-ahead log indexed by a single blob, reached a limit of writes in the mid-hundreds per second. Hashing references across several segment blobs raised the write limit, but every read then had to check every segment.

Compaction runs on separate nodes that lease a shard of the repository’s packs and merge them into larger ones. Each node checks that the new packs contain exactly the same objects before publishing them. The architecture is in a limited private preview, with a broader rollout planned for early next year. The follow-up list includes an atomic multi-file commit API, reading files straight from the server, and event streams.

Optimizing reference deletions in Git (Karthik Nayak) covers deleting refs in the files backend in repositories with millions of them, such as GitLab’s own with over 15 million. Deleting a packed ref rewrites the whole packed-refs file, which can reach several GB. Nayak had an LLM write a Rust version of the files backend to measure the overhead of the C to Rust boundary, and the Rust version deleted refs about 17% faster.

For every record being retained, the C code rebuilt the line with fprintf() and oid_to_hex(), where the Rust version copied the original bytes. Nayak’s patch writes retained records with fwrite() and matches the Rust version’s speed. It is merged and will ship in Git 2.98, the version number that follows 2.56, with Git 3.0 due two releases after that.
Releases

jj 0.47.0 adds a built-in :editor merge tool for jj resolve, which opens the conflicted file with conflict markers in a text editor and supports conflicts with more than two sides. Templates have a new top-level revset() function for evaluating revsets. In colocated workspaces, jj describe -r@ and jj restore --into=@ now preserve the Git staging area, and two race conditions with concurrent Git processes are fixed.

Updating remote-tracking Git refs in non-colocated workspaces moves from jj git fetch and push to jj git export. Timestamp.format() now uses jiff’s strftime syntax in place of chrono’s. 0.47.1 fixes a dependency error that broke Linux builds of 0.47.0, and deprecates the git.sign-on-push boolean in favour of a revsets.git-sign-on-push revset of the commits to sign.

GitButler 0.23.3 updates linked worktrees when the workspace is updated, and preserves conflicting uncommitted changes in them with conflict markers. It fixes branch apply, unapply and update writing encrypted files or Git LFS pointers in place of file contents in git-crypt and Git LFS repositories.

On the command line, but commit, amend, discard and diff accept Git-style paths, and but diff and but show take --stat. but commit runs Git commit hooks again in the main checkout. but push --dry-run lists the branches that would be refused and exits non-zero if there are any.

forges 0.3.2 adds providers for Entire and GitBucket, which brings the capability table to 14 forges. The Cursor Origin provider goes from 13 verified capabilities to 35, and the GitHub provider adds users.sponsorableMany. Two sourcehut fixes cover parsing web URLs on an instance’s root host and accepting a service host as baseUrl.

The Pushin changelog for 6 November (Peter, Pushin) adds branch and tag rulesets that can block history rewrites and deletion, and require a minimum number of approvals and passing workflow checks before a merge. Personal access tokens can now be scoped per permission group and limited to selected repositories. Existing tokens are migrated with full access and their expiry dates removed.

Webhooks are set up once per account or organisation and reused across repositories. The release also adds repository transfers that the new owner has to accept, runner groups shared across repositories, and Atom feeds for commits, releases, issues and pull requests.
Security
Git 2.56.1 (Elijah Newren, GitHub) fixes six vulnerabilities, with backports in 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3 and 2.50.2:

CVE-2026-111760: an integer truncation in index handling let an extremely long path pass validation under one name and be written under a shorter one. A malicious repository could use it to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symlink to a directory of attacker-supplied config or hooks, which then ran during a recursive clone.

CVE-2026-113408: when cloning an empty repository over protocol v2, a server could advertise a HEAD symref whose target contained path-traversal components. With the files ref backend, a later update to that branch could write outside the reference directory.

CVE-2026-114467: the code that strips GPG signatures from a message had a fixed-size stack array with room for two. Merging a tag with more than two wrote past the end of it, and hosting services that run merges for users are affected too.
CVE-2026-114469: the 1 GiB patch size limit checked only the size of the input, so a small binary patch that inflates past the limit caused an out-of-bounds read.
CVE-2026-105437: the size calculation for a merge result could overflow with many conflicts and a large conflict-marker-size, and Git then wrote outside the undersized buffer.

CVE-2026-114466: git fast-import now accepts rewrite-submodules-from, rewrite-submodules-to and export-pack-edges in an input stream only when the caller passes --allow-unsafe-features. The first two could read arbitrary files and the third could create or append to them.

GitHub has deployed the fixes on github.com and released GitHub Enterprise Server 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9 and 3.22.4. Git for Windows 2.56.1 includes the same six fixes, and GitHub says patched GitHub Desktop builds will follow.

lazygit 0.66.3 skips submodules whose name or path in .gitmodules resolves outside the repository. lazygit parses .gitmodules itself, and the pull request explains that removing a submodule named ../../../victim deleted the victim directory next to the repository. Anyone able to commit a .gitmodules file could set that up. Git skips such names, and lazygit now applies the same check and removes a submodule only when its git dir is inside .git/modules.

Gerrit 3.14.5 fixes a vulnerability where any user able to read a change could use on_behalf_of to act as a project owner and remove another reviewer’s vote. The release also speeds up tag listing by building the full tag details only for the page being returned. Listing 26 tags in a repository with 20,000 annotated tags went from around 450ms to between 15 and 35ms.
GitHub

A new pull request overview page is in opt-in public preview. It moves merge status to the top of the page in a redesigned merge box that takes less than half the space, with checks, comments and approvals summarised beside it. Conversations can be filtered to unresolved threads or the viewer’s own comments, and sorted newest first. A button in the header switches the preview on, and the same menu switches back to the classic page.

Secret scanning now covers GitHub Actions workflow logs in public preview, for GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers with Secret Protection or Advanced Security. Logs are scanned for provider patterns when a run completes, and the alerts are retained when the logs are deleted. Scanning is limited to provider patterns in logs from new runs, which excludes existing logs, generic patterns, custom patterns and secrets already masked by Actions.
Elsewhere

Anil Madhavapeddy is using Brief to power auto-CI in a new Tangled spindle. Brief is my tool for detecting the languages and toolchains in a repository. In the pipeline for Madhavapeddy’s xdge library, a detect workflow runs first, followed by an ocaml-ci workflow that builds on Debian 13 across several OCaml versions on x86_64 and arm64.
